title: Safe Use at Work: Privacy and Confidential Data

slide.title: Think Before You Paste
slide.body: Centre: clipboard icon with a teal shield and padlock. Three small labels underneath: Safe · Remove details · Never paste. Small tag: AI for Everyday Work · Lesson 3.

production_notes: [VERSION] Data-use, data-storage and model-training settings for free and paid plans of Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Gemini must be checked against current terms before recording. The voiceover stays hedged: text 'may be stored' and 'may be used to improve' the tool, 'depending on the tool, the plan and your settings'. Do not replace this with a specific claim about any product.

[VERSION] The description of business versions (Microsoft Copilot, Gemini in Workspace) and their data agreements must be checked against current product terms. The voiceover only says they 'can come with different data agreements'.
[VERSION] The statement that deleting a chat may not remove data already stored is kept hedged ('depending on the provider').
[REGION] Data protection laws and workplace AI rules differ by country and organisation. The voiceover gives no legal advice and points learners to their employer's policy.
Priya and her Pune insurance company are hypothetical; no real insurer's name or logo in stock footage.
Priya's rewritten prompt is shown in full on a code-layout slide (scene 12).

Hook.voiceover: It takes two seconds to copy a customer complaint, paste it into a chatbot and ask for a polite reply. It can take much longer to explain to your manager why that customer's name and account number are now in an outside tool.

Explain.voiceover: In this lesson, we look at safe use. When you type or paste text into an AI assistant, it is sent to the provider's computers. Depending on the tool, the plan and your settings, it may be stored for some time, and it may even be used to improve the tool.

slide.title: Where does your text go?
slide.body: Your computer → arrow → provider's computers (cloud). Under the cloud, two amber labels: 'may be stored' · 'may be used to improve the tool'. Footer: depends on tool, plan and settings.

Explain.voiceover: These settings are different on free and paid plans, and they change often. So you cannot assume that a free chat is private.
Explain.on_screen_text: Don't assume a free chat is private

Explain.voiceover: So, what should you never paste into a free, public AI tool? Personal data about customers, patients, students or colleagues, such as names, addresses, ID numbers, health or salary details. Passwords and access codes. Contracts that are not public. Unreleased financial figures, prices or plans. And anything your organisation marks as confidential or internal.

slide.title: Never paste into a free tool
slide.body: Personal data: names, addresses, ID numbers, health, salary · Passwords and access codes · Non-public contracts · Unreleased figures, prices, plans · Anything marked confidential or internal. Red stop icon.

Explain.voiceover: But some text is safe after you remove the details. Replace names with roles, such as the customer or colleague A. Remove numbers or round them, and describe the situation in general terms. The AI still helps with the wording, but no private data leaves your computer.

slide.title: Safe after removing details
slide.body: Before: '[Customer name], account [number], is upset…' → After: 'A customer is upset…'. Tips: names → roles · remove or round numbers · describe in general terms.

Explain.voiceover: Free consumer tools and company-approved tools are also different. Many organisations pay for business versions, such as Microsoft Copilot or Gemini in Workspace, which can come with different data agreements. Your IT or legal team decides which tools are approved, and for what data.

slide.title: Free tool or approved tool?
slide.body: Left: Free consumer tool (general use, personal account). Right: Company-approved tool (business version, chosen by IT or legal). Arrow to footer: Check which tools are approved, and for what data.

Explain.voiceover: That is why the first rule is always the same. Follow your employer's AI policy. If there is no policy, ask your manager before you use AI with work documents. Data protection laws also differ by country and region, and this course does not give legal advice. Your employer's policy is your best guide.

slide.title: Rule number one
slide.body: "Follow your employer's AI policy. No policy? Ask your manager first."

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple picture. Using a free AI tool is like talking about work in a busy public café. You can discuss general ideas, or how to word a polite reply. But you would not read a customer's file aloud at the next table.
Explain.stock_query: people talking in busy public cafe
Explain.on_screen_text: A free tool is a public café

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see this in practice. Priya is a claims assistant at an insurance company in Pune, in India. A customer has written an angry email about a late payment, and Priya wants help with a calm reply.
Demonstrate.stock_query: office worker reading email at desk

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, she checks her company's AI policy. It says staff may use the approved business tool for internal text, but must not paste customer data into free tools. Today Priya is using a free tool, so she does not paste the email.

slide.title: Priya checks the policy first
slide.body: Policy card: 'Approved business tool: internal text OK' · 'Free tools: no customer data'. Arrow: Using a free tool today → Do not paste the email (red cross over the email icon).

Demonstrate.voiceover: Instead, she writes a general prompt. A customer is upset because a payment is two weeks late. It is now approved and will arrive within five working days. She asks for a calm, polite reply of about one hundred words that apologises and explains the next step.

slide.title: Priya's safe prompt
slide.body: A customer is upset because an insurance payment is two weeks late. We have now approved it and it will arrive within 5 working days. Write a calm, polite reply of about 100 words that apologises and explains the next step.

Demonstrate.voiceover: She has removed the name, the policy number and the exact amount. The AI writes a good reply. Then Priya adds the customer's details herself, inside the company email system, and checks the whole message before she sends it.

slide.title: Details go in last, in the right place
slide.body: Step 1: general prompt (no name, no policy number, no amount) → Step 2: AI draft → Step 3: Priya adds details in the company email system → Step 4: final check → Send.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to think, it is only one email, nobody will read it. But the risk is data leaving the systems your organisation controls. And deleting the chat afterwards may not help, because depending on the provider, the data may already be stored.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, never paste personal data, passwords, contracts, unreleased figures or anything confidential into a free AI tool. Second, you can often still get help by removing names and numbers and describing the situation in general terms. Third, free tools and company-approved tools have different data terms, so always follow your employer's AI policy first.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Never paste personal or confidential data into a free tool. 2. Remove names and numbers; describe in general terms. 3. Follow your employer's AI policy first.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, sort ten example snippets of work text into safe to paste, safe after removing details, or never paste. Then find out whether your organisation has an AI policy, and note one rule from it. The next lesson is When AI Gets It Wrong: Checking Output. See you there.
